patterns: Rules guides converge on the same 8-12 rules: y+suffix, -es plurals, drop silent e, i-before-e, f→ves, consonant doubling, -ful/-ly, al-, q+u, -ck after short vowel, prefixes don't change the base.
Rules pages carry NO misspelled-word list; misspelled-word pages carry NO rules. No competitor fuses 'rule → the real-world words it saves you on → self-test'.

Hard-word listicles favour spelling-bee exotica (onomatopoeia, Worcestershire, fuchsia) rather than words adults actually type in emails (receive, schedule, colleague, acknowledge, occurred, separate, definitely).
Interactivity is mostly external (PDF via email capture, OTP-gated downloads, separate quiz pages). Grammar Monster is the only one with an on-page test.
Only Grammar Monster ranks words by real misspelling frequency; everyone else uses editorial picks.
Dates/authors are weak: 4 of 8 pages show no author or date; Leverage Edu and Testbook have visible factual errors.
Zero pages address Hindi/L1 interference (v/w, s/sh, dropped schwa, phonetic Hindi script leading to 'write as you say'), and zero address British-vs-American choice for Indian workplaces.
gaps_for_hindi_medium_adults_and_email_w: Phonetic-script transfer: Hindi is written as it sounds, so Hindi-medium learners write English the same way → 'untill', 'tommorow', 'goverment', 'seperate', 'definately'. No competitor explains this cause or gives a fix (anchor the silent/unstressed letter to a related word: govern-ment, de-finite-ly).

Pronunciation-driven errors specific to Indian English: v/w swaps (wery/very), s/sh (shedule), 'z' for 's' endings, -er/-or/-ar endings (calender, grammer, seperate), 'schedule', 'Wednesday', 'colleague', 'queue'.

Email-specific vocabulary audit: no page lists the 40-60 words that appear in Indian workplace emails and get misspelled (receive, acknowledge, occurred, accommodate, necessary, immediately, sincerely, regards, apologies, convenience, available, maintenance, recommend, until, business, calendar, address, schedule, liaise, guarantee, questionnaire, grateful, truly, argument, judgement).

British vs American choice: Indian companies default to British (colour, organisation, programme, licence/license, practise/practice) but Gmail/Outlook spell-check often defaults to US. Nobody tells readers how to set their spell-checker language or which standard to pick.

Spell-check blind spots: homophones and real-word errors (their/there, then/than, lose/loose, affect/effect, principal/principle, complement/compliment) that pass spell-check and reach a manager's inbox.
Hinglish/transliteration habits: SMS-style shortenings (pls, u, ur, thru, tmrw) leaking into formal mail; 'kindly do the needful' type phrasing is covered elsewhere but spelling-level leakage is not.
Adult-specific practice: the 'practice spelling' SERP is child-centric; an adult routine (5 words/day, say-cover-write-check on your own email drafts, dictate-then-type with an AI coach) is missing.
No speaking link: SpeakX can uniquely frame spelling through pronunciation (say it right → spell it right), which no competitor does.
